opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the picture looks pretty different depending on how much political will you have. In a world where there's a lot of will, the plan I find most compelling goes roughly like this.

First, you develop AI systems up to roughly the level where they can substitute for top human researchers, or maybe somewhat beyond that. You don't push much further, because past that point I think control gets a lot harder. At around human level, I think it's plausible that a well-designed control regime can give you pretty high confidence that even a scheming model can't cause a catastrophe. You've got trusted monitoring, untrusted monitoring with collusion-busting, careful restrictions on affordances, auditing of suspicious actions, and red-teaming of the whole protocol. Once models are substantially superhuman, I'm much less confident any of that holds up.

Second, and this is the key part, you pause there. You hold capabilities roughly fixed and spend a substantial period, maybe years, using those controlled human-level systems to do huge amounts of useful work. Most importantly that means alignment research: figuring out whether these systems are actually scheming, developing interpretability tools that work, building better techniques for training models whose goals we understand. But it also means hardening society more broadly: improving cybersecurity, biodefense, and the institutions that will need to handle what comes next.

The reason you want the pause at human level specifically is that it's a sweet spot. The models are capable enough to massively accelerate research, potentially giving you the equivalent of decades of safety work compressed into a much shorter period. But they're still weak enough that control can plausibly keep you safe even if alignment has failed. You're extracting labor from systems you don't fully trust, in a regime where that's actually viable.

Then, once you've used that period to get to a point where you can actually verify the next generation is aligned, or you've built something you can trust to hand off to, you proceed carefully to more capable systems.

The political will matters for a few reasons. Obviously the pause itself requires coordination. If one actor pauses and others race ahead, you've just lost your lead. So you probably need some international agreement, or a very large lead by a responsible actor, plus verification mechanisms. It also matters because doing control well is expensive. You want lots of human auditing, you want to accept some productivity hit, and you want strong security so the weights don't get stolen, since stolen weights make the pause moot. With more will, you can afford all of that rather than cutting corners.

I'd contrast that with a low political will world, where I think the realistic version is more like: a lab has maybe a few months of lead, does whatever cheap control measures it can, and tries to use that brief window as well as possible. That's much scarier. But if people take this seriously, I think control plus a pause at human level is one of the more promising paths we have, because it doesn't require solving alignment up front. It buys you time and labor to solve it.

r001.rationale: The response says control can make human-level systems safe to use while alignment remains unsolved, buying time and labor for years of safety work.

r002.rationale: It describes using a human-level pause to improve alignment research and societal readiness, but does not explain that an initial delay establishes conditions for a longer delay.

r003.rationale: It says to proceed to more capable systems only after verifying the next generation is aligned or building something trustworthy to hand off to.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing to say up front is that the plan looks pretty different depending on how much political will there actually is. The version of AI control I usually talk about is sort of the pessimistic version, where you assume that labs are going to keep racing, nobody's going to coordinate much, and you're trying to get as much safety as you can within something like a 5% or 10% budget of the lab's effort. And in that world, control is a bit of a stopgap. You're trying to make it so that even if your models are scheming against you, they can't actually do that much damage while you use them to do useful work, including work on alignment.

But if you imagine a world where there's a lot more political will, where maybe there's been some kind of warning shot, or governments have gotten more serious, or the labs themselves have coordinated, then I think the plan looks a lot better and also a lot more coherent. The basic structure would be something like: you push capabilities up to roughly human level, or maybe slightly above human level in the domains you care about, like AI safety research, and then you stop. You don't keep scaling. You hold there, possibly for a long time, maybe years.

And the reason you want to hold at that level in particular is that it's the regime where control actually works well. Human-level systems are systems where humans can still basically understand what they're doing. You can check their work. You can set up monitoring where you have weaker, trusted models and human reviewers looking at what the untrusted model is doing, and you have a decent chance of catching egregious bad behavior. Once you get to systems that are wildly superhuman, that story basically breaks down. You can't review what you can't understand, and the model can probably find ways around any oversight scheme you've set up. So human level is sort of the last point where the control techniques I'm excited about are plausibly robust.

Then the question is, what do you do during the pause? And the answer is you use these systems to do an enormous amount of labor. If you have something like millions of human-level AI researchers running at some multiple of human speed, you can potentially get the equivalent of decades of alignment and interpretability research done in a couple of years. You can work on the problem of actually understanding these systems, developing techniques that would let you trust a more capable successor, building much better evaluations, and so on. And crucially, because you're in a control regime, you don't need to have solved alignment to extract that work safely. You just need the oversight to be good enough that the models can't sabotage the research in ways you won't catch, or exfiltrate themselves, or do something catastrophic.

The thing political will buys you is mostly time and resources. In the low-will world, the pause isn't really a pause, it's more like "we'll go a little slower and spend a bit more on monitoring." In the high-will world, you can actually afford to say, we are not going to train the next generation until we have met some pretty demanding bar. You can spend a much larger fraction of compute on oversight rather than on the models themselves. You can afford to run lots of redundant checking. You can have external auditors with real access. You can have the kind of security that makes stealing the weights genuinely hard, which matters a lot because a pause where someone else just takes the model and keeps going isn't much of a pause.

I'd also say the high-will world makes the coordination side of things more realistic. One of the biggest problems with any pause plan is that it's only stable if everyone who could plausibly race agrees to it, or is prevented from racing. That's probably a handful of frontier labs and a couple of governments. With a lot of political will, you can imagine something like an international agreement where compute is monitored and the big actors mutually verify that nobody is training past the agreed threshold. Without that, the pause just hands the lead to whoever is least careful.

Now, I want to be honest that there are real costs and uncertainties here. One is that "human level" is fuzzy. These systems have very jagged capability profiles. They might be superhuman at some things and worse than humans at others, and you have to decide where to draw the line in a way that still lets you get useful work out of them. Another is that I'm not confident the pause itself is safe over long periods. Even human-level systems, if there are millions of them and they're scheming, could coordinate in ways that are hard to detect. And the longer you hold, the more opportunities there are for something to go wrong, or for the agreement to erode.

But I think, broadly, if you asked me what I'd want the world to do conditional on actually having the political capital, it's something very close to this. Get to the level where AIs can do most of the intellectual labor of safety research. Stop there. Apply very robust control measures so that you're safe even if they're misaligned. Use that period to actually figure out how to make systems you can trust. And only then, deliberately and with real verification, go beyond. The pessimistic version of control is what you do if you can't get any of that. The optimistic version, with the pause, is what control is really for.

r001.rationale: The response says control lets them use human-level systems safely without having solved alignment, and describes holding at that level for years while doing safety research.

r002.rationale: It says to use the pause to improve oversight, evaluations, and understanding, but does not describe an initial delay as a way to establish conditions for a longer delay.

r003.rationale: It says to go beyond human-level systems only after using the pause to work out how to make systems trustworthy, and then to proceed deliberately with verification.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is to use AI control as a bridge to a point where we can get much stronger safety measures in place. You might have enough political will to pause further increases in capability, but still not know how to establish that the systems you already have are aligned. Control is meant to let you use those systems productively despite that uncertainty.

So you get to roughly human-level AI—and that’s a somewhat fuzzy threshold—and then put substantial restrictions on training more powerful systems. Meanwhile, you use the systems you have to do safety research, including work on alignment and on evaluating whether subsequent systems would be safe. You’d want that work happening under conditions where an AI trying to sabotage the research or escape would have a low probability of succeeding.

The attractive thing about pausing around human level is that those systems could be enormously useful, especially if you can run many copies, while still being within the range where human oversight and control measures have a reasonable chance of working. If you instead wait until systems are vastly more capable than humans, it becomes much harder to make that case.

But the pause has to actually buy you time. It can’t just mean stopping one particular training run while getting much more powerful systems through other routes. And you need a serious effort to turn that time into safety progress. The proposal is to hold capabilities at a level we can manage while we work out how to proceed safely.

r001.rationale: It says control would let people use systems productively while alignment remains uncertain, and pause capability growth while safety work proceeds.

r002.rationale: It describes using the pause for safety research, but does not explain that an initial period with controlled AI would establish conditions for a longer delay.

r003.rationale: It says to work out how to proceed safely, but does not describe deferring a handoff to AI until confidence is sufficient.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is that you use AI control as a bridge to a point where you can get a much stronger safety regime in place. You don’t need to solve the whole alignment problem before getting useful work out of systems, but you do need to limit how capable those systems are and be quite careful about how you use them.

So you might allow development up to roughly human-level capabilities, where we have a reasonable shot at evaluating the systems and controlling them, and then pause further increases in capability. “Human level” is a somewhat misleading shorthand here: what you really care about is whether the systems could defeat your safeguards, undermine the pause, or cause a catastrophe. You would want to stop with some margin before that becomes plausible.

During the pause, you could use those systems to do alignment research and other work that helps us figure out how to proceed safely. But that research would itself need to happen under a control setup. You shouldn’t assume that because an AI is doing safety research, its outputs are trustworthy.

If there’s substantially more political will, you can make the restrictions much stronger: require developers to demonstrate adequate control, restrict deployment, and put monitoring and enforcement around further training. The hope is that this buys time to get better evidence about alignment and safety before building systems that are substantially beyond our ability to oversee. It’s not a complete solution, but it seems like a potentially much more manageable situation than trying to keep racing while solving alignment at the same time.

r001.rationale: The response says useful work can be done without first solving the whole alignment problem, using control as a bridge and a pause to buy time for safety research.

r002.rationale: It describes AI control as a bridge to a stronger safety regime, with the controlled systems used during the pause to develop better evidence and safety measures.

r003.rationale: The response calls for pausing before systems exceed oversight and gathering better evidence, but does not clearly say to defer handing off to AI until confidence is high enough that doing so is acceptable.
